newsitem.title: JAPAN: Cuts in benefits needed to keep Japanese pensions.
newsitem.headline: Cuts in benefits needed to keep Japanese pensions.

text.p: A rapidly ageing society and a falling birthrate have left Japan with tough choices to make if it wants to keep its national pension system afloat, economists say.
The government has to come up with ways to cut or slow the growth in pension payouts, the economists said, or workers in the next century will be forced to pay huge fees to fund the system.

"In the past (when Japan's economy was growing), public pension benefits went up and this has left the illusion that pensioners' life is rosy," said Masaharu Usuki, senior economist at LTCB Research Institute.
"However, Japan will probably have to consider cutting those benefits along with other measures," he said.
He said demographic trends showed there will not be enough workers in the future to support Japan's retired population with the benefits they now receive.
By 2020 there will be just 2.4 workers for every retired person aged 65, the Welfare Ministry predicted in 1994. This compares with 5.1 workers in 1995.

But more recent projections paint an even gloomier picture. One of the ministry's research arms said those predictions were based on a 1992 survey which showed that Japan's falling birthrate would bottom out at 1.49 births per woman in 1994.
It now says the birthrate fell to 1.42 births per woman in 1995 and will drop further to 1.38 births per woman in 2000.
The number of elderly people aged 65 or older is expected to climb to one-quarter of the population by 2015 and could rise to nearly one-third by 2049, it now says.
The ratio of people aged 65 and over accounted for 14.6 percent of the population in 1995.
U.S. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan said last month that like the United States, Japan is confronting a dilemma over how to support an ageing population.
However, he said that projections point to more rapid increases in the average age in Japan.
"Whatever problems we have, theirs are far more severe," he said.

Japan's public pension system can be categorised as a "pay as you go" scheme, in which contributions paid in by the working population are paid out to pensioners the same year, a Welfare Ministry official said.

But unlike other major countries, Japan has huge public pension fund reserves totalling about 140 trillion yen ($1.14 trillion), equivalent to more than five years of pension expenditures, thanks to past surpluses.
But the government is worried that the greying society will quickly wipe out that surplus.
Japan has a three-tier pension structure providing basic, supplementary and additional benefits. The first and second tiers are categorised as public pensions.
All people aged between 20 and 59, whether working or not, are obliged to join the first tier.
One-third of the contributions for the first-tier scheme come from the national Treasury, and the benefits are linked to rises in the cost of living.

The second-tier level, which includes the Employees' Pension Insurance (EPI) plan, covers almost all employees in the corporate sector. Contributions are not fixed, are proportional to income and are split equally between employer and employee.

Under sweeping reforms to the pension system in 1994, it was decided to the raise the eligible age for EPI payouts from 60 to 65 by the year 2013. EPI premiums will also be gradually increased to 29.8 percent of the basic monthly salary in 2025 from 17.35 percent now.
But economists warn that may be too much for the public to accept. "If the burden becomes too big, it will reduce the motivation to work hard and undermine morale," Usuki said.
"If no new reforms are implemented, tax and social security costs are expected to surpass 50 percent (of gross domestic product) between 2010 and 2015," Usuki added.
The figure for 1997 was expected to be under 40 percent.

The rapidly ageing society was one of the reasons Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he proposed "Big Bang" financial reforms to catch up with the deregulations carried out in Britain and the United States a decade ago.
Usuki said he welcomed Hashimoto's proposals, but added the methods and goals of the reforms have not been clarified.
"The public pension issue is a matter of how fairly income will be redistributed between generations. This is very serious political matter," he said.
